steps.text: The **king** is the piece you must protect. Its ordinary move is one square in any direction, straight or diagonal (castling is a special extra move you meet later). In the middle of the board it has eight squares, on an edge five, in a corner three. Watch it walk first, then try the edge yourself.

steps.text: Because the king must never be captured, the rules give it one extra rule: **a king may never step onto a square the enemy attacks.** A square is *attacked* when an enemy piece could capture on it, even if that piece happens to be pinned. The king may not end its move there, because it would be in check, and a king that cannot escape check is checkmated. A *rank* is a row of squares across the board; we start with the rook.

steps.text: **A habit to build** (a rule of thumb, not a law): take the king's neighbouring squares one at a time and ask, "If I stood here, which enemy piece could take me?" Rooks and bishops look along lines, and a line stops at the first piece in its way. The queen attacks like a rook and a bishop together. Knights jump, and pawns capture diagonally. [H] Beginners forget the pawn most often, because it moves straight but captures sideways. My guess, not data.

steps.text: [H] The rule that kings never touch is probably forgotten almost as often as the pawn rule, because it feels like a rule about distance rather than attack. Treat the other king like any attacker: it covers the eight squares around it. This is my guess, not data.

The king can also **capture**, but only a piece that is not guarded. A piece is **guarded** (also called defended) when a friendly piece could take back on its square, pinned or not. If the king took a guarded piece it would land on an attacked square, which is never allowed. Compare three knights.

steps.text: **Why bother with a careful king?** [S] Per our reading sheets of two classic books: Aron Nimzowitsch's *My System* teaches that in the endgame (when few pieces are left) the king should come to the centre and fight, and José Raúl Capablanca's *Chess Fundamentals* also gives king-march examples. [I] Both ideas need today's skill: a king can only fight on squares it may safely stand on.
One more thing before the quick ones: boards are sometimes turned so Black sits at the bottom. The rules do not change, only your view of them. Take the same careful look at each square.

steps.text: **Model answer.** The king steps one square in any direction, but never onto a square an enemy piece attacks and never next to the enemy king. Rooks, bishops and queens attack along lines that stop at the first piece in the way. Knights jump, pawns capture diagonally. The king may capture a piece only if nothing guards it. Before each king move I look at every neighbouring square and ask who could land there.
